promptText: A model shows training AUC of 0.94 but validation AUC of only 0.71. What does this gap most directly indicate, and what is a reasonable first fix?
options: High variance (overfitting); reasonable fixes include regularization, reducing model complexity, or gathering more training data
High bias (underfitting); the fix is to add more model capacity and train longer
The evaluation pipeline must contain a bug, since a gap this large is never caused by the model itself
This pattern indicates the learning rate is too low and should be increased substantially
explanation: A large train-validation gap where training performance is much stronger than validation performance is the classic high-variance symptom, addressed by regularization, simplifying the model, or adding more training data -- not by increasing capacity further.

promptText: Why does adding more regularization make an already-underfit model worse rather than better?
options: Underfitting means the model already lacks the capacity to capture the signal in the training data, so further constraining its weights removes even more of the limited expressive power it has, pushing it further from the true pattern
Regularization always improves any model regardless of whether it is overfitting or underfitting
Regularization only affects inference speed and has no effect on training or validation error
Underfit models cannot be regularized at all; the technique only applies to overfit models by definition
explanation: Overfitting and underfitting require opposite fixes -- regularization combats overfitting by constraining an overly flexible model, but applying it to an already too-rigid, underfit model further crushes its already-limited capacity to represent the underlying signal.

promptText: Geometrically, why does L1 (Lasso) regularization tend to drive some coefficients exactly to zero while L2 (Ridge) only shrinks them smoothly toward zero?
options: L1's constraint region has sharp corners aligned with the coordinate axes, so the optimum frequently lands exactly on an axis (a zero coefficient); L2's constraint region is a smooth sphere, so the optimum shrinks every coefficient a little without eliminating any
L1 and L2 use identical geometric constraint regions; the difference is purely in computational speed, not in which coefficients end up zero
L2 always produces sparser models than L1 because squaring weights forces small values to vanish entirely
L1 regularization can only be applied to classification models, while L2 can only be applied to regression models
explanation: The sharp-cornered L1 constraint region makes the optimal solution likely to land exactly on a coordinate axis (zeroing a coefficient), while L2's smooth spherical region causes uniform shrinkage of all coefficients without exact zeroing.

promptText: Why must a feature scaler (or imputer, or encoder) be fit only on the training fold and then applied unchanged to validation and test folds?
options: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting lets statistics from the validation/test data (their mean, variance, or correlations with the label) leak into training, producing an overly optimistic offline evaluation that will not hold up in production
Fitting a scaler on the full dataset is always faster and produces mathematically identical results to fitting only on training data
Scalers can only be fit on data that has already been through the model at least once during a prior epoch
This practice has no effect on evaluation validity; it is purely a coding style convention
explanation: Fitting data-dependent transforms on the full dataset before splitting is a form of train-test contamination -- a subtle data leakage pattern that inflates offline metrics without producing an error, making it especially dangerous.

promptText: A manufacturing defect-detection model reports 99.2% accuracy, but the true defect rate in the data is only 0.6%. Why should a stakeholder be skeptical of this headline number?
options: A trivial always-predict-no-defect baseline would already score about 99.4% accuracy, so 99.2% may represent a model that is barely better than doing nothing useful at catching the rare positive class
99.2% accuracy is impossible to achieve on any real dataset, so the number must be the result of a bug
Accuracy is always the correct metric regardless of class balance, so no further investigation is needed
The defect rate of 0.6% is irrelevant to interpreting accuracy since accuracy only depends on the total number of predictions made
explanation: On heavily imbalanced data, accuracy can look impressively high while a trivial majority-class baseline achieves nearly the same score -- the real question is recall on the rare positive class, which accuracy alone completely obscures.

promptText: Why do tree-based models like random forests and gradient boosting generally not require feature scaling, unlike k-NN or SVMs?
options: Trees split on threshold comparisons of one feature at a time, which are invariant to monotonic rescaling, so the relative order of values within a feature -- not their absolute scale -- is what determines the split
Tree-based models internally normalize every feature automatically before the first split, making external scaling redundant
Feature scaling is harmful to tree-based models and will always reduce their accuracy if applied
Trees only ever use categorical features internally, so numeric scale has no meaning for them
explanation: Since a tree split just asks whether a feature value is above or below some threshold, monotonic rescaling (like standardization) doesn't change which points fall on which side of that threshold, making trees invariant to feature scale.

promptText: Why does the curse of dimensionality specifically degrade the performance of distance-based algorithms like k-NN and k-means as the number of features grows?
options: In high-dimensional spaces, the ratio of volume near the edges to total volume approaches 1, so points that were meaningfully close or far in low dimensions tend to become roughly equidistant from each other, undermining any notion of a meaningful nearest neighbor
Distance-based algorithms become computationally impossible to run at all once more than 10 features are used
High dimensionality only affects gradient-based optimizers, never algorithms that rely purely on distance calculations
The curse of dimensionality is purely a storage problem and has no effect on the mathematical meaningfulness of distances
explanation: As dimensionality increases, distances between points converge, weakening the geometric notion of 'nearest neighbor' that k-NN and k-means fundamentally rely on -- a geometric fact, not a modeling choice, that directly undermines those algorithms.

promptText: A dataset contains multiple monthly snapshots per customer, and a model is validated using plain random 5-fold cross-validation, reporting a strong 0.88 AUC. Why is this number likely unreliable, and what should be used instead?
options: Rows from the same customer's different months can be split across train and validation within the same fold, leaking that customer's outcome pattern into training; GroupKFold, grouping by customer ID, prevents this
The 0.88 AUC is fully reliable as reported; grouping by customer would only be relevant for time-series forecasting problems, not this scenario
Stratified k-fold is required here instead, since the only issue is class imbalance, not grouped records
Random 5-fold CV is always more reliable than GroupKFold regardless of data structure, since more folds average out any leakage automatically
explanation: Without grouping, near-duplicate information from the same customer leaks across the train/validation boundary within a fold, producing an inflated score -- GroupKFold by customer ID prevents this specific leakage pattern.

promptText: What is the fundamental mechanistic difference between how random forests and gradient boosting reduce error?
options: Random forests train many deep trees independently on bootstrapped samples and average them, primarily reducing variance; gradient boosting trains shallow trees sequentially, each correcting the residual errors of the ensemble so far, primarily reducing bias
Random forests and gradient boosting use mathematically identical training procedures and differ only in their default hyperparameter values
Random forests reduce bias by training trees sequentially, while gradient boosting reduces variance by averaging independent trees
Gradient boosting can only be used for regression tasks, while random forests can only be used for classification tasks
explanation: Random forests decorrelate independently-trained deep trees via bagging and feature randomness to cancel variance through averaging, while gradient boosting sequentially fits shallow trees to the current ensemble's residuals, primarily driving down bias.

promptText: What mathematical property of SVM optimization does the kernel trick exploit to avoid ever explicitly computing a high-dimensional feature mapping?
options: The SVM's optimization and decision function depend on the data only through pairwise dot products, so a kernel function can compute the equivalent inner product in the transformed space directly, without ever materializing the transformation itself
The kernel trick works by physically reducing the dataset's dimensionality before training begins, rather than operating on dot products
SVMs do not actually use any dot products internally; the kernel trick instead replaces gradient descent with a closed-form matrix inversion
The kernel trick eliminates the need for a margin-maximizing hyperplane entirely by using a lookup table of precomputed labels
explanation: Because the SVM's math depends on the data only through dot products, replacing that dot product with a kernel function gives the effect of an (even infinite-dimensional) transformation without ever computing it explicitly.

promptText: A network-intrusion detection model reports 0.97 ROC-AUC but floods a security team's triage queue with false positives in practice. What explains this discrepancy, and what metric would have surfaced it earlier?
options: ROC-AUC's false positive rate is computed against the huge pool of true negatives, so even a large absolute number of false positives can register as a tiny rate on heavily imbalanced data; PR-AUC, which computes precision relative to predicted positives, would have revealed the operational problem
ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are mathematically identical metrics, so no alternative metric could have revealed this issue
The discrepancy means the model's ROC-AUC score of 0.97 must have been computed incorrectly, since a high ROC-AUC always guarantees low false-positive volume
The security team's complaint is unrelated to the evaluation metric and must stem from a UI issue in the alerting dashboard
explanation: On heavily imbalanced data, ROC-AUC's false-positive-rate denominator (the huge negative class) can mask a large absolute volume of false positives; PR-AUC directly reflects precision among predicted positives, exposing the operational reality ROC-AUC hid.

promptText: What do residual/skip connections do specifically to address vanishing gradients in very deep networks?
options: They give gradients a direct, unattenuated path backward that bypasses the multiplicative chain-rule product through intermediate layers, which is central to why very deep ResNets and Transformers can be trained at all
They eliminate the need for backpropagation entirely by computing gradients using only forward passes
They work only by increasing the learning rate automatically whenever a gradient becomes very small
They convert all activation functions in the network to linear functions, which removes gradient multiplication altogether
explanation: Because backpropagation multiplies per-layer gradient factors across many layers, a direct skip-connection path lets gradient signal flow backward without being repeatedly shrunk by that multiplicative chain, directly combating vanishing gradients in deep networks.

promptText: A team scales training from one GPU to a multi-GPU cluster, increasing batch size proportionally but keeping the original learning rate unchanged. Validation accuracy drops even though training loss looks the same. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: This is the large-batch generalization gap -- larger batches give less noisy gradients that tend to converge to sharper, less-generalizing minima at a fixed learning rate; applying the linear learning-rate scaling rule with a longer warmup typically recovers validation performance
The drop must be caused by a bug in the multi-GPU data-parallelism implementation, since batch size has no theoretical connection to generalization
Larger batch sizes always improve generalization, so the correct explanation is that the validation set itself must have changed between runs
The fix is to decrease the batch size back to its original single-GPU value while keeping multi-GPU hardware active, since batch size and hardware count must always match exactly
explanation: Larger batches reduce gradient noise, which acts less as an implicit regularizer and can lead to convergence at sharper minima that generalize worse under the same learning rate -- the linear scaling rule plus longer warmup is the standard mitigation.

promptText: A production model's accuracy drops sharply overnight with no corresponding code deployment. What is the recommended order of investigation, and why does it start where it does?
options: First confirm the degradation is real (not a measurement artifact), then check upstream data/feature pipeline changes, then training-serving skew, then genuine distribution/concept shift, and only last suspect the model or code itself -- because the large majority of sudden production incidents trace back to boring, common causes like upstream data changes, and model/code bugs are usually caught by pre-deployment testing already
Immediately retrain the model with the latest available data, since retraining is always the fastest way to resolve any sudden accuracy drop regardless of root cause
Immediately roll back to a more complex model architecture, since sudden drops in accuracy are always caused by insufficient model capacity
Assume the drop is due to concept drift and skip directly to root-causing changes in the real-world relationship between features and target
explanation: Starting from 'boring and common' (measurement artifacts, upstream data/feature changes) and working toward 'rare and dramatic' (the model itself) reflects where most real production incidents actually originate, and avoids wasted effort chasing an architecture change when the true cause is often an upstream pipeline bug.

promptText: A model's ground-truth churn labels take 30 days to become confirmable. How can a team detect a real-world problem with the model before those labels are available, and why are feature/prediction drift signals treated as complementary to, not a replacement for, eventual ground-truth performance monitoring?
options: Feature drift (input distribution shift) and prediction drift (output score distribution shift) can be measured immediately and serve as earlier warning signals during the label-delay window, but ground-truth performance monitoring remains the most trustworthy signal once labels arrive, since distribution shifts don't always translate into an actual accuracy problem
There is no way to detect a problem before ground-truth labels arrive; teams must simply wait the full 30 days before any monitoring can begin
Feature drift monitoring makes ground-truth performance monitoring completely unnecessary once it is set up, since distribution shift always implies an equivalent performance drop
Prediction drift can only be measured after ground-truth labels are available, since it requires comparing predictions to actual outcomes
explanation: Feature and prediction distribution monitoring provide faster, if less precise, warning signals during the label-delay window, while ground-truth performance monitoring -- available only once labels arrive -- remains the most trustworthy but slowest signal, making the two complementary rather than substitutes.
